evidence.text: Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”
Jesus replied, “It is also written: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’”
“Away from Me, Satan!” Jesus told him. “For it is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”
When Jesus heard that John had been imprisoned, He withdrew to Galilee.
From that time on Jesus began to preach, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”
As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
“Come, follow Me,” Jesus said, “and I will make you fishers of men.”

c: Simon Peter

Simon Peter was the most prominent of the twelve apostles. After Jesus’ death, he became the primary spokesman for the early Christians in Jerusalem and was the apostle primarily responsible for evangelizing the Jews (
The Hebrew name
Simeon
(transliterated in English as “Simon”) was probably his original name.
Cephas
is the transliteration of an Aramaic name given him by Jesus, meaning “rock”—translated in Greek as
Petros
(English “Peter”; see
Though Bethsaida was Peter’s hometown (
), he later lived in Capernaum. He was married (
), and at one point, when visiting Peter’s home, Jesus healed Peter’s mother-in-law (
Originally fishermen, Peter and his brother Andrew were among the first to be called by Jesus to be disciples, together with James and John, their fishing partners (
; cp.
). They were ordinary, minimally educated working men (
Peter’s name occurs first on every list of the twelve apostles (
). Together with the brothers James and John, Peter was part of an “inner circle” of disciples who were with Jesus on certain special occasions—the healing of Jairus’s daughter (
), Jesus’ transfiguration (
), and Jesus’ prayer in the garden (
Peter was bold and impulsive (
), and the first of the disciples to confess his belief in Jesus as the Messiah (
). He reproved Jesus when Jesus spoke of his coming death—a notion that did not fit Peter’s view of the Messiah—and was in turn rebuked by Jesus for it (
). However, Jesus spoke of Peter as a key person he would use to build the church (

Peter surreptitiously entered the courtyard of the high priest when Jesus was taken there for interrogation. But when challenged by people who recognized him (partly because of his Galilean accent), he vigorously denied all knowledge of Jesus (
)—as Jesus had said he would, in spite of Peter’s insistence that he would never do so (
). Peter immediately felt deep remorse.
After the news of Jesus’ resurrection, Peter was one of the first to run to the tomb to see if it was true (
), and he appears to have been the first of the Twelve to whom the risen Jesus showed himself (
). Much of Jesus’ conversation recorded in
was with Peter, whom Jesus encouraged to “feed my sheep” (
Following the coming of the Holy Spirit on the Day of Pentecost (
), Peter quickly emerged as the primary spokesman for the early Christians. From that point on, as recorded in
, he played a crucial role in the spread of the gospel in Judea, boldly preaching to the crowds (
), healing people (
), and—even under arrest—speaking fearlessly to the authorities (
). Twice he miraculously escaped from prison (
). He also exercised leadership in the administrative affairs of the quickly growing community of disciples (
Peter was the first to bring the Good News to Gentiles (
; see

). And he played a key role in the Jerusalem council concerning Gentile converts, arguing that Gentiles should not be compelled to observe the law of Moses but should be accepted on the basis of their faith in Christ alone (
). Later, however, when visiting Antioch, he was inconsistent on this point—resulting in a rebuke from Paul (
Other than his taking his wife with him on at least some of his mission trips (
), few details are known about Peter’s later life and missionary work. (He may have spent time at Corinth; see
). Widespread early tradition says that Peter was crucified—like his Lord, just as Jesus had predicted (
)—in Rome during Nero’s persecution of Christians in
AD
64–65. The reliability of the tradition that he was crucified upside-down is less certain.

Peter was likely the source of the material recorded by Mark in his Gospel, which Mark probably learned while he was assisting Peter in his evangelistic work in Italy near the end of his life. Peter is also traditionally understood to be the author of 1 Peter (written from Rome—“Babylon,”
) and 2 Peter.

In the New Testament, Peter stands as a reassuring example of Christ’s forgiving grace for those who know they’ve failed him—and of the way Christ can graciously restore and use such people for his glory, in spite of their failings.

was a federation of ten cities, most of which were east of the Jordan and southeast of the Sea of Galilee (Damascus, Raphana, Hippos, Abila [or Canatha], Gadara, Scythopolis, Pella, Dion, Gerasa, and Philadelphia [Amman]). These cities were predominantly Gentile and Hellenistic in culture.
